title: Taras Bulba on Comradeship
text:
In Nikolai Gogol's novel, the old Cossack colonel Taras Bulba led his men in a campaign against the Poles. The Cossacks were besieging the city of Dubno, and things were going badly. Many of their number had left to pursue a raiding party of Tatars who had attacked their home camp, and those who remained were expecting a hard battle against a strong enemy.

Before the fighting, Taras gave his men a speech about what bound them together. A father loves his child, he said, and a mother loves her child, and a child loves father and mother. But even a beast loves its young. To be kin by the soul and not by blood was something only a human being could do. Such brotherhood had existed in other lands, he told them, but nowhere as it existed among the Cossacks. He asked them to stand together and to show what Cossack comradeship meant.

The Cossacks, moved by his words, went into the battle. They fought hard, and many of them fell, among them old friends of Taras. In the end Taras himself lost both of his sons in the war: Andriy, who had gone over to the Poles and whom Taras killed with his own hand, and Ostap, who was captured and executed by the enemy.
lesson: Bonds chosen through shared struggle can be as strong as family ties. A leader who names what holds a group together can help it stand in the hardest hour.
people: Taras Bulba, the Cossacks, his sons Ostap and Andriy
location: Russian Empire (novel set in Ukraine and Poland)
source: Nikolai Gogol, Taras Bulba (1842 edition), chapter 9
